920:
An apprenticeship is a formal, structured arrangement in which a person learns a skilled trade or profession — not by sitting in a classroom, but by actually doing the work, side by side with an experienced expert, over a set period of time.

Think of it this way: instead of reading about how to build a house, you go and build one — but with a seasoned builder standing next to you, guiding you, correcting your mistakes, and passing on everything they know. That entire experience, from start to finish, is the apprenticeship.
The Three Pillars That Define It

Every true apprenticeship rests on three things working together:

Learning by doing. The heart of an apprenticeship is hands-on, real-world practice. The apprentice is not a student sitting at a desk — they are actively performing the job, handling real tools, real clients, and real challenges from day one.

Guidance from an expert. The learning happens under the close supervision of someone who has already mastered the skill. This person — sometimes called a master, mentor, or journeyman — is not just a supervisor. They are actively teaching, demonstrating, and shaping the apprentice's skill.

A formal agreement over time. An apprenticeship is not casual. It is typically a structured contract between the apprentice, the expert (or employer), and sometimes the government. It lasts a fixed period — often anywhere from one to five years — and ends with the apprentice being recognized as competent or qualified in that trade.

At the beginning, the apprentice knows very little. They observe, assist with simpler tasks, and make many mistakes — and that is perfectly expected. The mistakes are part of the learning.

As time goes on, they are trusted with more complex tasks. Their skill grows gradually, in layers, because they are practicing daily in real conditions — not simulated ones.

By the end, they can perform the trade independently and confidently. In many systems, they receive a formal certificate or qualification proving they have completed the apprenticeship.

Importantly, apprentices are usually paid a wage during their training, even though it is lower than what a fully qualified worker earns. This is one of the things that makes apprenticeships special — you earn while you learn.

Apprenticeships are used across a wide range of fields:

Traditionally, the word is most closely associated with skilled trades — carpentry, plumbing, electrical work, masonry, metalwork, tailoring, and similar crafts. These are jobs where physical skill and technical precision are built only through practice, and an apprenticeship is the historical and still-popular path into them.

In the modern world, apprenticeships have expanded into many other fields too — accounting, healthcare, technology, culinary arts, engineering, and even law. Many large companies and governments now run official apprenticeship programs as an alternative to university.
How It Differs From Similar Things

Apprenticeship vs. Internship: These are easy to confuse. An internship is usually shorter (weeks or a few months), often unpaid or minimally paid, and focused more on exposure to a workplace than on deep skill-building. An internship rarely ends with a formal qualification. An apprenticeship is longer, paid, much more structured, and ends with recognized competence in a specific trade or profession.

Apprenticeship vs. Going to College/University: In college, you learn theory in a classroom and may practice in simulated environments. An apprenticeship flips this — the primary learning happens on the job, in real conditions. Some modern apprenticeships do combine some classroom learning with work, but the work always comes first.

Apprenticeship vs. Simply Being Employed: A regular job means you are already qualified and are being paid for your contribution. An apprenticeship acknowledges that you are still learning — the work is the training itself.

The word is also commonly used in a broader, non-formal sense to describe any long period of learning under someone else's guidance — even without a contract.

For example: "Her years assisting the veteran editor served as her apprenticeship in the craft of writing." Here, no formal agreement exists, but the meaning is clear — she spent a formative period learning from an expert through direct experience.

This figurative use captures the spirit of the word beautifully: deep, mentored, practical learning that shapes a person's abilities over time.
Common Ways the Word Is Used in Sentences

To complete/finish an apprenticeship — "He completed his apprenticeship as an electrician at age 22."

To serve an apprenticeship — "She served a four-year apprenticeship under one of the city's best chefs."

To begin/start/undertake an apprenticeship — "He decided to undertake an apprenticeship instead of going to university."

An apprenticeship in something — "She did an apprenticeship in carpentry."

An apprenticeship program/scheme — "The company runs a two-year apprenticeship program for school leavers."

An apprenticeship is the formal process of learning a skilled trade or profession by doing it in the real world, under the close guidance of an expert, over a set period of time — after which you emerge as a qualified, capable practitioner.
921:
To apprise someone means to inform or notify them about something — to make sure they know about a fact, a situation, or a development.

When you apprise someone, you are deliberately bringing important information to their attention so they are not left in the dark.

This word almost always follows one fixed pattern:

apprise + person + "of" + information

You always apprise someone of something. The word "of" is glued to it. Examples:

  • "She apprised her manager of the problem."
  • "The officer apprised the general of the enemy's movements."
  • "Please apprise me of any changes."

If you drop the "of," the sentence breaks down. So treat "apprise of" as a pair that travels together.
The Tone: It's a Formal Word

"Apprise" lives in formal territory. You'll find it in professional emails, legal documents, news reports, and official communication — not usually in casual everyday conversation. If a friend tells you about a party, they "tell you" or "let you know." But if a lawyer informs a client about a court ruling, they might "apprise" them of it.

This formality is part of the word's identity. Using it signals a level of seriousness and officiousness.

These examples will show you the word doing its job in real sentences:

  • At work: "The CEO apprised the board of directors of the company's financial losses."
  • In medicine: "The doctor apprised the patient of all possible risks before the surgery."
  • In law/government: "The intelligence agency apprised the president of the developing threat."
  • Casually formal: "I'll make sure to apprise you of the situation as it unfolds."
  • Passive form: "She was apprised of the decision late Friday evening." (meaning: she was informed of it)

This is the single most common mistake people make with this word, and it's worth understanding clearly.

AppriseTo inform someone
AppraiseTo evaluate or assess something (its value, quality, or condition)

Examples side by side:

  • "The agent appraised the painting." → The agent assessed its value.
  • "The agent apprised the owner of the painting's value." → The agent informed the owner.

The two words sound similar and are spelled almost the same, but they mean entirely different things. A jeweler appraises a diamond ring (judges its worth). A jeweler apprises you of what the ring is worth (tells you the result).

One of the most common ways you'll encounter this word is in the phrase "keep someone apprised of" — meaning to continuously update someone as new information comes in, not just inform them once.

  • "Please keep me apprised of any new developments."
  • "The field team kept headquarters apprised of conditions on the ground."

This phrase implies an ongoing flow of information, not a single moment of being told something.

To apprise someone = to formally and deliberately inform them of something important, using the structure apprise + person + of + information.

That's the word, fully unpacked. Simple in meaning, formal in tone, and always followed by "of."
922: Approach means to move closer to something or someone — but not all the way there. There is always a sense of moving toward, of getting nearer, rather than arriving. This sense of "closing a gap — but not completely closing it" runs through almost every use of this word.
The Four Main Ways "Approach" Is Used as a Verb

1. To physically move toward something or someone

This is the most straightforward use. You are somewhere, and you move in the direction of a person, place, or thing.

"She slowly approached the dog."
"The ship approached the harbour."
"A stranger approached him on the street."

What makes "approach" special here: It implies deliberate, steady movement — not a sudden lunge or a sprint. There is intention in the movement. Compare: you don't "approach" something by accident; you approach it with some awareness of what you're moving toward.

Also notice that approach implies distance still exists at the moment of description. The moment you arrive, you stop approaching. So approach captures that in-between state — the journey toward, not the destination.

2. To nearly reach a number, level, or quality

Here, "approach" is used when something is almost equal to a value — but not quite.

"The temperature approached 45°C." (It got very close to 45, maybe 44.5)
"His skills approach those of a professional."
"Losses approached a billion dollars."
"The crowd approached ten thousand."

The key idea: something is getting close to a threshold or standard without necessarily crossing it. It's a way of saying "nearly" or "almost" — but with more precision and power.

This is commonly used with numbers, measurements, and abstract qualities like perfection, greatness, or genius.

"No other writer has approached Shakespeare's mastery of language."

Here it means: no one has come as close to his level.

3. To go to someone and speak to them about something

When you "approach" a person, you are initiating contact with them for a specific purpose — to ask them something, request something, propose something, or discuss something.

"She approached her manager about a pay raise."
"They approached the government for funding."
"He was afraid to approach her with the idea."
"The club approached the player about joining their team."

What makes this special: It carries a slightly formal, deliberate tone. You are not just talking to someone — you are going to them with an agenda or a need. There is usually some care or thought involved in this approach, because you are initiating something that matters.

In passive voice, this is very common:

"She was approached by a producer who wanted to make her story into a film."

(Someone came to her with a proposal.)

Also note: when someone "approaches" you, it often implies that whatever they want requires your agreement or cooperation — a job offer, a request, a deal, a collaboration.

4. To begin dealing with something — to handle or tackle it in a certain way

This is one of the most important uses. When you "approach" a task, problem, situation, or topic, you are choosing a way to begin and handle it — often with a particular attitude, method, or strategy.

"How should we approach this problem?"
"She approached the exam calmly and methodically."
"He approached the conversation with care."
"They approached the issue from a completely different angle."

The key idea here: The word is not just about doing something — it's about the way you begin and engage with it. Your approach shapes everything that follows.

This is why you often see phrases like:

  • "approach with caution"
  • "approach with an open mind"
  • "approach differently"
  • "approach from a new angle"

These all tell you how someone is entering and handling a situation.
A Deeper Feel for the Word

Across all four uses, one thread connects them: intentional movement — physical, intellectual, or social — toward something, with awareness and purpose.

Whether you are walking toward a building, a number getting close to a target, asking your boss for something, or deciding how to handle a difficult conversation — in every case, something is moving toward something else in a measured, deliberate way.

The word "approach" often carries a sense of care or caution. You don't usually "approach" something recklessly. There is a mindfulness to it.

Compare:

  • "He ran up to the bear." — reckless, thoughtless
  • "He cautiously approached the bear." — measured, aware

Even in professional contexts:

  • "Approach the subject carefully." — treat it with sensitivity

This careful, purposeful quality is baked into the word.
When Someone Is the Object (Passive Voice)

When a person "is approached," it means someone has come to them — usually with a request, offer, or purpose.

"The scientist was approached by three universities offering her a job."
"He was approached by a journalist wanting to know his side of the story."

This phrasing is very natural and very common in English.

Approach + [a place or person]
→ Moving toward them physically, or making contact with them for a purpose.

Approach + [a number or level]
→ Getting close to that value, but not necessarily reaching it.

Approach + [a problem, task, or topic]
→ Deciding how to handle or begin dealing with it.

Approach + [an adverb or "with" phrase]
→ Describes the manner in which you are engaging: "with caution," "carefully," "from a new angle," "differently."

Approach vs. Reach:
Approach = moving toward, still some gap.
Reach = you've arrived, you've made it.

"The rocket approached the satellite." (still closing in)
"The rocket reached the satellite." (it got there)

Approach vs. Contact:
Approach sounds more deliberate, personal, and often implies some delicacy or care.
Contact is neutral and can be impersonal (email, phone, text).

"She approached the director in person." (more personal, intentional)
"She contacted the director by email." (neutral, impersonal)

Approach vs. Tackle:
Both can mean dealing with a problem, but:
Approach = how you begin and engage with something — the mindset and method.
Tackle = actively and energetically engaging with something — getting into it.

"We need to approach this problem differently." (rethink our method)
"We need to tackle this problem immediately." (get into it and work on it)

UseWhat it means
PhysicalMove closer to something/someone
Numbers/QualityGet close to a value or standard
SocialGo to someone with a request or proposal
Tasks/ProblemsHandle or engage with something in a certain way

The verb "approach" is one of those quietly powerful words in English. It shows up wherever there is movement — physical, intellectual, or social — toward something, with care and intention. Once you feel that core idea clearly, you will recognise and use this word naturally in almost any context.
923: "Approachable" means easy to reach, talk to, or engage with — without fear, nervousness, or difficulty. Think of the word "approach," which means to come near to someone or something. When you add "-able" to it, it simply means capable of being approached comfortably. Something or someone approachable doesn't push you away — it pulls you in.

This is the most common use of the word. A person is approachable when they make others feel comfortable enough to walk up and talk to them.

An approachable person seems open, warm, and non-intimidating. They don't make you feel judged, dismissed, or unwelcome. You don't hesitate before going up to them — you just feel at ease doing it.

For example, imagine two managers at a company. One has a serious, cold expression, rarely smiles, and seems too busy to be disturbed. The other makes eye contact, smiles naturally, and seems genuinely interested in people around them. The second manager is approachable. Even if both managers are equally skilled, only one feels safe to talk to.

Here is an important nuance: being approachable is not the same as simply being "nice" or "kind." A person can be secretly very kind but still come across as distant, intimidating, or hard to reach — which makes them unapproachable. Approachability is about the impression someone gives and the actual ease with which others can connect with them. It lives at the intersection of warmth, openness, and accessibility.

Approachable people tend to have certain qualities that make them feel this way — a relaxed and open body language, a calm and welcoming tone, patience when others speak to them, and a non-judgmental attitude. They are the kind of people others seek out when they have a problem or a question, because there is no fear of rejection or awkwardness.

Common examples of how it is used about people:

  • "She is one of the most approachable professors I have ever had — I never feel embarrassed asking her a question."
  • "Despite being the CEO, he is surprisingly approachable."
  • "The new coach has an approachable personality, so the players feel free to speak their mind."
When Used About Things (Subjects, Books, Ideas, Art, etc.)

"Approachable" doesn't only describe people. It is widely used to describe subjects, books, writing styles, music, food, concepts — basically anything that could be easy or difficult for someone to engage with, understand, or get into.

When a complex topic is explained in a simple, clear, and beginner-friendly way, we say it has been made more approachable. When a book doesn't require expert knowledge to enjoy, it is an approachable book. When a style of cooking doesn't intimidate a beginner, it is an approachable cuisine.

The key idea here is: the barrier to entry is low. You don't need a special background, expertise, or courage to engage with it.

For example:

  • "This documentary makes quantum physics feel approachable — even a ten-year-old can enjoy it."
  • "The author writes in an approachable style — no complicated jargon, just clear and honest language."
  • "Italian food is often considered one of the most approachable cuisines in the world."
  • "The band's music is catchy and approachable, even for people who don't usually like jazz."

In all of these cases, the word signals the same thing: this is not intimidating, not difficult, not exclusionary — it is open to you, wherever you are starting from.

Understanding a word's opposite often sharpens your understanding of the word itself.

The opposite of approachable is "unapproachable." A person who is unapproachable feels cold, distant, intimidating, or simply too important or too busy to be spoken to. You might have a question for them, but something about them makes you hold back.

Similarly, an unapproachable subject is one that feels overwhelming, overly complex, or requires so much background knowledge that a newcomer feels instantly lost or discouraged.

Being approachable does NOT mean being:

  • A pushover or someone without authority
  • Unprofessional or too casual
  • Simple or lacking depth

A doctor can be highly skilled and authoritative and still be completely approachable — patients feel comfortable describing their symptoms honestly. A book can be intellectually rich and still be approachable if it is written clearly. The word carries no negative connotation whatsoever. It is always a compliment.

Like most adjectives, approachable comes in degrees. You can be slightly approachable, very approachable, or surprisingly approachable (meaning more so than expected). Writers often intensify or soften the word with adverbs:

  • "She is incredibly approachable for someone in her position."
  • "The topic becomes more approachable once you understand the basics."
  • "He tries to seem approachable, but he's still a little intimidating."

If someone asks you what "approachable" means, the simplest and truest answer is: it describes something or someone that is easy, comfortable, and non-intimidating to go near, talk to, or engage with.

Whether it is a teacher who makes every student feel welcome to ask questions, a complicated science book written in plain everyday language, or a dish that anyone can enjoy without being a food expert — the word "approachable" captures that universal quality of being open, accessible, and inviting to those who encounter it.
924:
Approbation means approval — but not just any quiet, internal approval. It means approval that is expressed, shown, or officially given. It is the act of endorsing something or someone with clear, positive recognition.

Think of it this way: if you simply feel good about something in your head without saying or doing anything, that is not quite approbation. But the moment that approval is communicated — through words, a gesture, a formal decision, or open praise — that is approbation.

The word is used in two closely related but slightly different ways:

1. Official or Formal Approval
This is when an authority, institution, or person in power formally sanctions or endorses something. It is approval in an authoritative, sometimes even legal or ceremonial sense.

"The plan could not move forward without the king's approbation."
"The new medicine received the committee's approbation after years of testing."

Here, approbation is less about warmth and more about sanctioned permission — a stamp of legitimacy from someone who has the power to give it.

2. Expressed Praise or Warm Endorsement
This is when someone openly shows that they admire, appreciate, or are pleased by something or someone. It is approval with a positive emotional charge — closer to commendation or acclaim.

"She looked to her father's face, hoping to find some sign of approbation."
"The audience showed its approbation with thunderous applause."

Here, it is more personal and emotionally meaningful — the approval of someone whose opinion matters to you.
How It Differs From the Word "Approval"

"Approval" and "approbation" are close cousins, but approbation carries a slightly different weight:

  • Approval is the everyday word. It is neutral and practical. ("I got my manager's approval to take the day off.")
  • Approbation is more formal and carries a richer sense — often implying that the approval is enthusiastic, earned, or official, and that it matters deeply to whoever is receiving it. It suggests the approval is not just permitted but celebrated or validated.

Approbation also tends to appear in more formal, literary, or elevated writing. It is the kind of word you will encounter in a novel by Jane Austen, in a legal document, in a formal speech, or in serious journalism — not typically in casual conversation.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

An important thing to understand is that approbation is often tied to a desire for it. In literature and formal writing, characters and people are frequently described as seeking, craving, or earning approbation. This captures something deeply human — the need to be validated, praised, or endorsed by others, especially by people we respect.

"He spent his whole career working for the approbation of a mentor who rarely gave it."

This gives the word a psychological depth that plain "approval" sometimes lacks.

• It is not mere tolerance — tolerating something is not approbating it.
  • It is not passive acceptance — approbation is active. It is expressed and communicated.
  • It is not secret or private — by its nature, approbation is outward-facing. You give approbation to someone or something.

The clearest opposite of approbation is disapprobation — which means expressed disapproval or condemnation. Other opposites include censure, condemnation, and reproach. Knowing this helps solidify the meaning: if disapprobation is harsh criticism or rejection, then approbation sits on the other end — open, positive endorsement.

Here is how the word naturally appears in sentences:

  • "meet with approbation" — to be received positively
    "His speech met with widespread approbation."*
  • "earn/win approbation" — to gain approval through effort
    "She finally won the approbation of the critics."*
  • "give/grant approbation" — to formally or openly approve
    "The board gave its approbation to the merger."*
  • "seek/crave approbation" — to desire approval from others
    "He was a man who constantly sought the approbation of those around him."*
  • "nod/sign/token of approbation" — a gesture or signal of approval
    "The professor gave a small nod of approbation when she answered correctly."*

• Approbate (verb, rare/formal) — to officially approve something
  • Approbatory (adjective) — expressing approval (an approbatory nod)
  • The much more common everyday verb is simply approve, and the everyday noun is approval

Approbation is the formal, expressed approval or praise of something or someone — often from an authority or someone whose opinion carries weight — communicated openly rather than simply felt in private.
925:
Appropriate means suitable or fitting for a specific situation, person, place, time, or purpose.

When something is appropriate, it is the right thing — the thing that matches, fits, or belongs in that particular context. It is not too much, not too little. It feels correct given everything around it.

"That was an appropriate response."
"Please wear appropriate clothing to the ceremony."
"This book is appropriate for young readers."
The Most Important Idea: It Is Always Relative

This is the single most important thing to understand about "appropriate": it never means suitable in an absolute, universal sense. It always means suitable for something specific — a situation, an audience, a time, a purpose, a place.

The same behavior, word, or thing can be appropriate in one context and completely inappropriate in another.

Example 1:
Laughing loudly is appropriate at a comedy show. The exact same behavior — loud laughing — is inappropriate at a funeral. The behavior itself didn't change. The context changed.

Example 2:
Using very technical, advanced medical language is appropriate when a doctor speaks to another doctor. The same language is inappropriate when that doctor speaks to a worried patient who doesn't have medical training — not because it's wrong, but because it doesn't fit the audience.

Example 3:
Asking someone "What's your salary?" might be appropriate during a job negotiation. The same question would be inappropriate if you asked a stranger you just met at a party. Again — same words, different context, different judgment.

So whenever you see or use the word "appropriate," your brain should automatically ask: appropriate for what? For whom? In which situation?
What Creates the Context? What Makes Something "Fit"?

Several factors together decide whether something is appropriate:

1. The occasion or situation
A formal business meeting calls for different language, clothing, and behavior than a casual birthday party. What fits one doesn't fit the other.

2. The audience
A joke that is appropriate among close friends might be deeply inappropriate in front of your boss or your grandmother. The same joke, different audience.

3. The relationship
It is appropriate to hug a close friend when you meet them. It is not appropriate to hug a stranger you've just been introduced to.

4. The time
It is appropriate to call a friend at 3 in the afternoon. Calling them at 3 in the morning — unless there's an emergency — is not.

5. The place or setting
Loud music is appropriate at a party. The same volume is inappropriate in a library or a hospital.

6. Social, cultural, or professional norms
Different societies, workplaces, and cultures have their own shared standards of what fits and what doesn't. What is considered appropriate in one culture may be seen as odd or rude in another.

When we call something appropriate, we are making a judgment — we are saying it meets a certain expected standard for that context. This standard is often shared: society, culture, a profession, or a community has collectively decided what is fitting.

This is why "appropriate" sometimes feels like it has a light moral or ethical weight. It's not just about personal preference. It's about whether something meets an expected standard.

"That was not appropriate behavior for the classroom."

This sentence implies the classroom has a standard of expected behavior, and the person's behavior fell outside that standard. It is a social or institutional judgment, not just an opinion.

"Appropriate" has several close relatives, but each one has its own flavor:

  • Suitable — Almost identical in meaning. Often used when something practically fits a purpose or need. "These boots are suitable for the rain." Very interchangeable with "appropriate," but slightly less judgmental in tone.
  • Fitting — Emphasizes harmony or match. It has a slightly more poetic or emotional feel. "It was a fitting tribute to her life." — meaning it matched, it honored the occasion beautifully.
  • Proper — Stronger sense of correctness, often relating to etiquette, formality, or official standards. "Proper behavior in court." "Proper" often implies there is a correct rule or established norm being followed.
  • Apt — Used especially for words, descriptions, comparisons, or remarks. It means not just suitable but precisely right, often in a clever or insightful way. "That was an apt description."
  • Relevant — Means directly connected or related to the matter at hand. "Please keep your questions relevant to the topic." "Relevant" is more about logical connection than social fit.
  • Pertinent — Similar to relevant, but slightly more formal. Means directly applicable to the issue being discussed.
  • Befitting — Slightly formal or literary. Means "suitable for someone or something of a particular status or character." "A celebration befitting a champion."

The direct opposite of appropriate is inappropriate — meaning not suitable, not fitting, out of place.

Other antonyms include: unsuitable, unfit, improper, out of place, ill-suited, irrelevant, inapt.

Like many adjectives, "appropriate" can be qualified — things are not always fully appropriate or fully inappropriate. There is a range:

  • Perfectly appropriate — fits exactly, ideally suited
  • Entirely appropriate — fully fitting, no doubt
  • Appropriate enough — good enough for the purpose, even if not ideal
  • Somewhat appropriate — fits reasonably well but not perfectly
  • Not entirely appropriate — slightly off, a mild problem
  • Barely appropriate — just within the acceptable range
  • Hardly appropriate — almost crossing the line
  • Completely inappropriate — totally out of place, violates the expected standard

"Appropriate" appears very frequently in these patterns:

Adjective + noun combinations (most common):

  • appropriate behavior — the conduct expected in a given situation
  • appropriate language — words that fit the setting (no slang in a formal report; no jargon with a beginner)
  • appropriate action / measures — the right steps to take
  • appropriate response — a reply or reaction that fits the situation
  • appropriate attire / clothing / dress — clothing that fits the occasion
  • appropriate content — material suited to the audience (often used regarding age)

Compound adjectives with "appropriate":

  • age-appropriate — suitable for someone of a particular age ("age-appropriate movies for children")
  • culturally appropriate — fitting within a specific cultural context
  • context-appropriate — tailored to the specific situation

Common sentence structures:

  • "It is appropriate to [do something] when [situation]."
  • "[Something] is appropriate for [a person/occasion/purpose]."
  • "Is it appropriate to [do something] in this situation?"
  • "Please use language appropriate for [audience/setting]."
  • "The teacher took appropriate action."

Common verbs used with "appropriate":

  • deemed appropriate — judged to be suitable (often by an authority)
  • considered appropriate — thought to be fitting
  • find/found appropriate — think something fits the situation
  • seem appropriate — appears to be fitting
A Subtle But Useful Note: "Appropriate" as a Polite Way to Criticize

In everyday English, "appropriate" is often used indirectly — as a polite, softened way to say something was wrong or off, without using harsh words.

Compare:

  • "That comment was rude and offensive." ← Direct and strong
  • "That comment was not entirely appropriate for this setting." ← Softer, more professional

Both sentences express disapproval, but the second one does so more diplomatically. This is why you often see "appropriate" (and "inappropriate") in formal, professional, or institutional language — in workplaces, schools, official statements — where people need to flag a problem without sounding aggressive.

Appropriate = fitting, suitable, and right for the specific context.

It is never about something being good or bad in absolute terms. It is always about whether something matches the situation, the audience, the time, the place, and the expectations of that moment.

When something is appropriate, it belongs there. It does not stand out awkwardly. It does not offend, confuse, or misfit. It slots in correctly, like the right key in the right lock.

When something is inappropriate, it violates the expected standard — it jars, it clashes, it doesn't belong. The situation called for something different.

The more clearly you understand the context — who is involved, what is happening, what the norms are, what purpose is being served — the more clearly you can judge whether something is appropriate or not.
926:
When "appropriate" is used as a verb, it means to take something and make it your own — either by claiming it, using it, or officially setting it aside for a purpose.

Notice the spelling is the same as the adjective ("appropriate behavior"), but the meaning is completely different. The adjective means suitable or fitting. The verb means to take or claim something. Context always makes it clear which one is being used.

Meaning 1: To take something — often without full right or permission

This is the most common and important use of the verb. When someone appropriates something, they take it and use it as their own — sometimes unfairly, sometimes without asking, and sometimes without even realizing they're doing something wrong.

The key feeling the word carries is this: the thing being taken belonged somewhere else first.

Examples:

  • A manager takes a junior employee's brilliant idea, presents it in a meeting, and gets the credit. → He appropriated his colleague's idea.
  • A student copies chunks of someone else's writing and puts it in their own essay. → She appropriated passages from another author's work.
  • A powerful country takes over land that belonged to another group of people. → The colonizers appropriated the land from its original inhabitants.

In all these cases, notice the sense of claiming or seizing — something was taken from its rightful place and absorbed into someone else's ownership or use.

Important nuance: "Appropriate" doesn't always mean the taking was violent or illegal. It just means something was claimed in a way that raises questions about fairness or right. The word is neutral enough to describe both outright theft of ideas and more subtle forms of taking.

Meaning 2: To officially set aside money or resources for a specific purpose

This meaning is used mainly in formal, legal, or governmental contexts. Here, "appropriate" doesn't have a negative tone at all. It simply means to designate or allocate something — usually funds — for a particular use.

Examples:

  • The government decides to spend a certain amount of money on building new roads. → Congress appropriated funds for road construction.
  • A company's board sets aside a portion of the budget for employee training. → The board appropriated $2 million for staff development.

Here, the word means: "We have officially decided that this resource is now assigned to this specific purpose." Think of it like putting money into a labeled envelope — it's been claimed for one job and cannot be used for anything else.
The One Thing Both Meanings Share

Even though the two meanings feel different on the surface, they share the same deep logic:

Something is taken, claimed, or assigned — and it now "belongs" to a specific person, group, or purpose.

In Meaning 1, the claiming is often informal and questionable. In Meaning 2, the claiming is formal and authorized. But in both cases, something is being pulled toward a particular owner or use.

Once you understand "appropriate," the word misappropriate becomes easy. It simply means to appropriate wrongly — especially to take money or resources that were meant for one purpose and use them for something else, usually dishonestly.

  • A charity treasurer uses donation money to pay for personal vacations. → She misappropriated the charity's funds.
Cultural Appropriation — A Phrase Worth Knowing

You will very often hear the phrase "cultural appropriation" in modern discussions. This is built directly on Meaning 1 of the verb. It refers to when people from one culture take elements — music, clothing, language, traditions, spiritual practices — from another culture (often a minority or historically oppressed one) and use them without proper understanding, respect, or credit.

For example, if someone from outside a particular indigenous community begins selling that community's sacred symbols as fashion accessories for profit, that is widely described as cultural appropriation. The elements of that culture have been appropriated — taken and used by those who don't belong to it.
How to Spot the Verb in a Sentence

Since "appropriate" looks identical as both a verb and an adjective, here's a simple trick:

  • If the word is followed by a noun (a thing being taken), it's the verb. → "She appropriated the funds."
  • If the word describes whether something fits or is suitable, it's the adjective. → "That was an appropriate response."

To appropriate something (verb) means:

  1. To take it and claim it as your own — often when you don't fully have the right to, whether that's someone's idea, land, culture, or creative work.
  2. To formally set it aside for a specific purpose — especially money or resources, in official or government settings.

The heart of the word is always the same: something is being claimed. The tone — whether questionable or perfectly legitimate — depends entirely on the situation.
927:
"Appropriately" means in a way that fits the situation perfectly — in a manner that is right, suitable, and correct for the specific circumstances at hand.

Think of it this way: every situation in life has invisible rules or expectations about how things should be done. When someone acts in a way that matches those expectations, they act appropriately. When they don't, they act inappropriately.

The word answers the question: "Was it done in the right way for this situation?"
The Key Insight: Context Is Everything

What makes this word so interesting is that what counts as "appropriate" shifts completely depending on the situation. There is no single standard. The rightness or suitability is always measured against the specific context.

For example:

  • Wearing a swimsuit is appropriately dressed at the beach. The same swimsuit at a funeral is not appropriately dressed — it's inappropriate.
  • Laughing loudly is appropriately expressive at a comedy show. At a library, it's not.
  • Speaking softly is appropriately quiet in a hospital. At a cricket match, you'd barely be heard.

The action itself (wearing clothes, laughing, speaking) isn't good or bad on its own. The word "appropriately" tells you that the manner of doing it matched what the situation called for.
What Kind of Word It Is, and How It Works

"Appropriately" is an adverb, which means it describes how something is done. It modifies verbs, adjectives, and other adverbs.

  • She dressed appropriately for the interview. (modifies a verb — describes how she dressed)
  • He responded appropriately to the criticism. (describes how he responded)
  • The punishment was appropriately severe. (modifies an adjective — tells you the severity was just right)
  • She spoke quite appropriately for the occasion. (modifies another adverb)
The Full Range of What It Can Mean

Because "appropriate" covers suitability across many dimensions, "appropriately" can refer to:

Behaviour and conduct:

The students behaved appropriately during the ceremony.

This means they acted in the way expected of students in that setting — quietly, respectfully, attentively.

Tone and language:

She spoke to her boss appropriately.

She used respectful, professional language — not too casual, not rude, not overly formal either.

Timing:

He arrived appropriately early for his job interview.

Not so early it was awkward, not late — just the right amount of early.

Amount or degree:

The charity was appropriately funded for the size of the project.

The money given matched what the project actually needed — not too little, not wastefully excessive.

Reaction or response:

She appropriately expressed concern when she heard the bad news.

Her emotional response fit the gravity of the situation. She didn't laugh, she didn't overreact — she responded in the way any thoughtful person would.
The Idea of an Invisible Standard

When someone says something was done "appropriately," they are measuring the action against some standard or expectation — a benchmark of what should happen in that situation.

This standard can come from:

  • Social norms (how people generally expect others to behave in a given setting)
  • Professional rules (how a doctor, teacher, or lawyer is expected to act)
  • Moral expectations (what a fair, honest, or kind person would do)
  • Practical requirements (what the task actually requires to succeed)

The engineer appropriately tested the bridge before opening it to the public.

Here, the standard is practical and safety-based. Testing before opening is what the situation demanded. Doing it was appropriate; skipping it would have been inappropriate and dangerous.

Like most adverbs, "appropriately" can be strengthened or softened:

  • Quite appropriately — clearly suitable, with some emphasis
  • Very appropriately — strongly fitting, especially noteworthy
  • Appropriately enough — used when the fitting nature of something is slightly ironic or unsurprising: "Appropriately enough, the award for best environmentalist was made from recycled materials."
  • Not entirely appropriately — a soft, polite way of saying something was a little off

Understanding "appropriately" becomes crystal clear when you look at its opposite. "Inappropriately" means doing something in a way that does not fit the situation — it's wrong, unsuitable, or out of place.

  • He inappropriately made jokes during the memorial service.
  • She inappropriately wore a party dress to a job interview at a law firm.
  • The teacher inappropriately shared a student's private information with other students.

Every time you see "inappropriately," the message is: this did not match what the situation called for, and usually there's a sense that the person should have known better.

One important nuance: who gets to decide what's "appropriate"? The answer is that it depends on the context. Sometimes society broadly agrees (shouting at a newborn baby's crib is inappropriate — nearly everyone would agree). But sometimes it's debatable.

Was his response to the criticism appropriately direct, or was it rude?

One person may say it was appropriately direct and honest. Another may say it crossed a line into rudeness. This is why you'll sometimes hear people argue over whether something was appropriate — because appropriateness is measured against standards, and people don't always share the same standards.

This doesn't mean the word is vague. It just means the word honestly reflects the way human judgement works.
How It Feels in a Sentence

"Appropriately" carries a quiet sense of approval and rightness. When you use it, you are not just describing what happened — you are gently confirming that it should have happened that way. There is a small note of satisfaction or validation in the word.

The firefighter appropriately prioritised rescuing the trapped child first.

The word "appropriately" here does more than describe the order of rescue. It signals: yes, that was the right call. That's how it should be done.

Compare to just saying "The firefighter rescued the trapped child first." That's a neutral fact. Adding "appropriately" is a quiet verdict: that was correct and fitting.

What it meansIn a way that fits, suits, or is right for the situation
What it depends onThe context — the situation, the setting, the expectations
What it signalsA quiet approval that the manner matched what was needed
Its oppositeInappropriately (done in a way that doesn't fit)
Its root adjectiveAppropriate (fitting, suitable, right for the context)

(Apologies — a small reference summary slipped in. The core explanations above are the substance.)

That is the complete picture of "appropriately." Its power lies in the idea that rightness is always relative to context — and this word is the elegant way English says "yes, it matched."
928:
Appropriation means the act of taking something and making it your own — setting it aside for a particular person, group, or purpose. The key idea baked into the word is that something is being claimed, allocated, or taken — sometimes with full authority to do so, and sometimes without.

Because this word lives in several different worlds (law, government, culture, and art), it can feel slippery. But once you understand its core engine — something being taken or set aside for a specific use — each meaning will click into place naturally.

1. The Everyday, General Meaning

In its most basic sense, appropriation is the act of taking something for your own use, often without asking permission. The thing being taken doesn't have to be a physical object — it can be an idea, a phrase, a style, or credit for someone else's work.

His appropriation of his colleague's research, without giving her any credit, was considered deeply unethical.

Here, he took something that wasn't his — not physically, but intellectually — and claimed it as his own. That act of taking-and-claiming is the appropriation.

Notice that this sense carries a negative tone. When used this way, it implies the taking was wrong, unfair, or at least questionable.

2. The Government and Financial Meaning

This is probably the most "official" and neutral use of the word, and you'll see it often in news about budgets and governments.

In this context, appropriation means the formal, official act of setting money aside for a specific purpose. A government body (like a parliament or congress) "appropriates" funds — meaning it officially decides that a specific amount of money will go toward a specific use and no other.

The government's appropriation of $2 billion for flood relief ensured the money could only be spent on that disaster and nothing else.

This meaning is almost always neutral or positive in tone. It simply describes a formal, legitimate process. The money isn't stolen — it's officially designated.

A helpful image: think of it like labelling a jar. The act of appropriation is the moment someone writes "FLOOD RELIEF" on the jar and puts the money inside. That money now belongs to that purpose.

3. Cultural Appropriation

This is the use you'll most commonly encounter in social and political conversations today, and it is always loaded with serious weight.

Cultural appropriation refers to when a person or group adopts specific elements from a culture that is not their own — its music, fashion, hairstyles, spiritual practices, language, food, or art forms — especially when they do so without proper understanding, respect, or acknowledgment, and often while the people of that original culture are discriminated against or disadvantaged.

The reason this causes controversy is the power imbalance at its core. It tends to happen when a more dominant or privileged group takes from a historically marginalized or oppressed group. The group doing the taking often receives praise, profit, or recognition for something that members of the original culture were (or still are) mocked, penalized, or excluded for.

Wearing a sacred ceremonial headdress as a Halloween costume is widely considered cultural appropriation.

Some critics accused the fashion brand of cultural appropriation for selling expensive versions of traditional handwoven textiles from an indigenous community, without crediting or compensating those artisans.

Why does it matter? Because the original culture often gets nothing — no credit, no money, no respect — while someone from outside takes the thing and profits from it or turns it into a trend. Meanwhile, the people from that culture may still face prejudice for the same things being celebrated when an outsider does them. That gap — between how the original culture is treated versus how the borrower is treated — is what makes this form of appropriation harmful in most people's eyes.

It's worth noting: not everyone agrees on exactly where the line is, and the debate around cultural appropriation is genuinely complex. Some argue that all cultures have always borrowed from each other, and that sharing is natural and even good. Others argue that context, power, and respect are what separate harmful appropriation from respectful cultural exchange. Both sides of this debate use the word "appropriation" — one to criticize it, and the other sometimes to challenge whether a particular act really qualifies.

4. Appropriation in Art

In the art world, appropriation has a specific technical meaning: the deliberate use of existing images, objects, or artworks within a new work of art, usually with the intention of commenting on, questioning, or transforming the meaning of the original.

This is largely a neutral to positive term in artistic circles. Famous artists have built entire careers around it.

Andy Warhol's paintings of Campbell's soup cans are a classic example of artistic appropriation — he took a mass-produced commercial image and placed it in a fine art context, asking the viewer to think differently about both.

The point of artistic appropriation is usually intellectual: the artist is making a statement about the original image or object by lifting it out of its original context and placing it somewhere new. It's intentional, creative, and often provocative.
Tone: When Is It Negative, Neutral, or Positive?

The same word carries very different emotional weight depending on context:

ContextTone
Taking someone's work or ideas without permissionNegative
Government allocating fundsNeutral / Positive
Taking from another culture without respectNegative / Contested
Using existing art to create new meaningNeutral / Positive
The Thread That Connects All Meanings

Even though appropriation appears in such different conversations, all its meanings share one DNA:

Something is being taken or claimed — and the question is always whether that taking is legitimate, respectful, and fair.

When the answer is yes (as in a government budget), the word is neutral. When the answer is no — or at least questionable — the word becomes a word of criticism and moral weight.

Once you internalize that core tension, you'll never be confused by appropriation again, no matter where you encounter it.
929:
Approval means a positive response toward something or someone — a signal that says "yes, this is good" or "yes, you may go ahead." It captures the idea of finding something acceptable, correct, or pleasing, whether that comes from a feeling inside you or from an official decision by an authority.

The word works in two main directions: one is emotional (how you feel about something), and the other is official/formal (a decision made by a person or organization in power). Both share the same core: something has been judged and found to be okay, right, or good.

1. An Expression or Feeling That Something Is Good

This is the personal, emotional sense. When you look at something and feel that it is right, pleasing, or satisfactory — and you show that feeling — you are expressing approval.

This kind of approval doesn't require any formal process. It can be a smile, a nod, a word of praise, or simply a positive attitude toward something.

Examples:

  • She looked at her son's drawing and smiled in approval.
  • He glanced at the new employee's work with quiet approval.
  • The crowd cheered in approval when the singer walked on stage.
  • The teacher's nod of approval made the student feel confident.

Here, approval is about a person's judgment or reaction — not a legal or official act.

2. An Official Decision That Allows Something to Happen

This is the formal, authoritative sense. When a company, government, boss, bank, or any authority officially agrees to let something happen — after examining it — that is called an approval. In this sense, it is often the final step before something can start or be used.

Without this approval, the thing often cannot proceed. It is a kind of green light from someone in a position of power.

Examples:

  • The new medicine has not yet received government approval.
  • She submitted her project plan and is waiting for the manager's approval.
  • The loan approval came through, so they could buy the house.
  • Building a new bridge requires approval from several departments.

In everyday business, legal, and administrative life, this sense of approval is everywhere. It carries a sense of gatekeeping — the power to say "yes" officially.
Approval as a Feeling Someone Seeks from Others

One very common and psychologically important use of "approval" is when a person wants others to think well of them — to validate them, accept them, or consider them good enough. This is deeply human.

When someone is described as seeking approval, it means they care greatly about what others think of them and want to be liked, praised, or accepted.

Examples:

  • He always tried to dress well because he craved approval from his peers.
  • She found it hard to make decisions without her mother's approval.
  • As a child, all he wanted was his father's approval.

This usage often appears in discussions about psychology, self-confidence, and relationships. Needing too much approval from others is often seen as a sign of insecurity. Acting freely without needing others' approval is seen as a mark of self-confidence.

"Approval" can be used both ways, and the meaning shifts slightly.

Uncountable (no "a" or "an," no plural): This is the general feeling or act of approving. It refers to the concept or quality.

  • "She smiled in approval." (the feeling itself)
  • "The idea won widespread approval." (the general positive reception)

Countable (can say "an approval" or "approvals"): This refers to a specific, individual act of formally approving something.

  • "The project needs three separate approvals before it can begin."
  • "Each approval takes around two weeks to process."

These fixed phrases appear very often in English and are worth knowing:

Stamp of approval / Seal of approval:
When something receives the "stamp of approval," it means it has been officially accepted or endorsed — often by someone whose opinion matters. The phrase comes from the image of literally stamping a document to mark it as accepted.

  • "The recipe got the stamp of approval from the head chef."

Nod of approval:
A nod of approval is a gesture — a small, positive movement of the head — that shows you agree or are pleased. It is also used figuratively to mean any quiet, informal sign of acceptance.

  • "The director gave a nod of approval after watching the rehearsal."

On approval:
This is used in commerce. When goods are sent "on approval," the buyer receives them, examines them, and can return them if they are not satisfied — paying only if they decide to keep them.

  • "The antique dealer sent the vase on approval so the client could decide."

Win someone's approval / Gain approval:
To succeed in making someone accept or be pleased by something.

  • "It took months to win the board's approval for the new plan."

Withhold approval / Deny approval:
To refuse to give the formal go-ahead.

  • "The bank withheld approval because the applicant's income was too low."

Seek approval:
To actively try to get someone's agreement, permission, or positive judgment.

  • "She sought approval from the committee before launching the campaign."

Not all approval is the same. Here are some varieties you'll encounter:

  • Enthusiastic approval — strong, excited agreement ("The crowd greeted the announcement with enthusiastic approval.")
  • Tacit approval — approval that is not stated openly but is understood from someone's silence or inaction. If you don't object, it may look like you approve.
  • Reluctant approval — when someone agrees, but unwillingly ("He gave his reluctant approval to the plan.")
  • Conditional approval — approval that comes with strings attached ("The loan received conditional approval — they would lend the money only if she provided a guarantor.")
How "Approval" Is Different from Similar Words

Several words are close in meaning but not identical. Understanding the differences will sharpen your grasp of "approval."

Approval vs. Permission:
Permission is specifically about allowing someone to do something. Approval is broader — it can be about judging the quality of something, expressing satisfaction, or granting authorization. Every permission involves a kind of approval, but not every approval is a permission.

  • "She gave her permission for him to leave early." (he asked to leave; she allowed it)
  • "She expressed her approval of his decision." (she judged it and found it good — no action was necessarily being allowed here)

Approval vs. Consent:
Consent is specifically about agreeing to something that will happen to you, or that affects you personally. It carries a strong sense of personal agreement and is especially used in legal, medical, and ethical contexts. Approval is more general and can apply to third-party situations too.

  • "The patient gave consent for the surgery." (it's happening to them)
  • "The committee gave approval for the project." (they are evaluating something, not necessarily something that affects them directly)

Approval vs. Endorsement:
An endorsement is a public, often enthusiastic declaration of support — usually from someone well-known or respected. Approval is quieter and more general. An endorsement is a strong, public form of approval.

  • "The celebrity's endorsement of the product boosted its sales."
  • "The teacher's approval meant a lot to the student."

Approval vs. Acceptance:
Acceptance means something has been received or taken in — it is more passive. Approval involves making a positive judgment. You can accept something without fully approving of it.

  • "She accepted his apology." (she received it, moved on)
  • "She approved of the way he had handled the situation." (she judged it and found it good)
A Summary to Tie It All Together

Approval is the noun that captures the idea of judging something and finding it to be good, acceptable, or satisfactory — or of officially authorizing something. It lives in two worlds at once: the personal world of feelings and reactions, and the formal world of institutions, decisions, and power.

When a parent looks proudly at their child, when a government clears a drug for use, when a boss signs off on a budget, when an audience erupts in cheers — all of these involve approval in some form. What they share is this: something was looked at, judged, and found to be good enough to receive a "yes."
